outcome: No progress on the question of whether there are infinitely many Lucas primes has been found since 26 January 2024; it remains an open conjecture with no rigorous proof for any Lucas sequence except the trivial cases.
summary: The question of whether infinitely many Lucas primes exist (Lucas numbers Lₙ that are themselves prime) is a long-standing open conjecture in number theory, analogous to the open questions for Fibonacci primes and Mersenne primes. It is a special case of the broader open problem of whether Lucas sequences Uₙ(P,Q) contain infinitely many prime terms: besides the trivial sequences Uₙ(2,1)=n and Uₙ(-2,1)=(-1)^(n+1)n, no Lucas sequence has ever been rigorously proven to contain infinitely many primes, though heuristic (probabilistic/Hardy-Littlewood-style) arguments support the conjecture for most coprime (P,Q). Broderius and Greene's related conjecture (that every Lucas sequence not in one of two specific exceptional families has infinitely many prime terms) remains itself unproven. I searched broadly for any 2024–2026 work bearing on this: (1) the Wikipedia 'Lucas number' article, which states the largest confirmed Lucas prime is L₁₄₈₀₉₁ (Sept. 2015, 30,950 digits) and largest known probable prime is L₅₄₆₆₃₁₁ (Aug. 2022), with no updates since; (2) The Prime Pages (t5k.org) 'Lucas Number' top-20 list, whose most recent entries (V(202667), V(193201), V(183089), V(159521)) all date to November–December 2023, i.e. before the frozen revision, with no post-window additions found; (3) OEIS A001606 (indices n with Lₙ prime), whose most recent substantive discovery comment dates to 2017; (4) recent arXiv papers on Lucas sequences (e.g. 'Shifting Lucas Sequences Away From Primes', INTEGERS 25 (2025); 'On members of Lucas sequences with bounded prime gaps', J. Number Theory 2025) address related but distinct questions — constructing sequences with few/no primes, or bounding prime gaps among Lucas-sequence members — none of which settle or narrow the infinitude question for the classical Lucas sequence itself, so under §3.1 these are related-problem results rather than progress on this bullet; (5) the Wikipedia 'List of mathematical discoveries by artificial intelligence' page, which comprehensively tracks AI-driven results on prime-related conjectures (e.g. OpenAI's bound improvement on the twin-prime-gap problem, DeepMind's work on Erdős problems, Anthropic's work on Riemann zeta zeros) and contains no mention of Lucas primes or Lucas sequences at all. I found no claim, preprint, announcement, or computational record update — by a human or an AI system — that changes what a careful person would write in this bullet's entry. This matches the triage's 'none' verdict; I did not find any evidence to disagree with it, though I additionally verified the record-table angle (largest known Lucas prime) explicitly to rule out even a narrow reading of 'progress', and per §3.1 that record axis is not the relevant one for an existence question regardless.
competing_reading: None of the record-table facts (largest known Lucas prime/probable prime) would count as progress on this bullet even if a new record had appeared post-window, since per §3.1 an infinitude question is not advanced by exhibiting one more example. No plausible alternative classification presents itself here.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (or disproof) that some non-trivial Lucas sequence, or the classical Lucas sequence Lₙ specifically, contains infinitely many primes — or a preprint/announcement claiming such a proof, which would then need expert digestion to move from claimed to resolved.
